questions.question: What is the key difference between an interface and an abstract class in Java?
questions.title: Interface vs Abstract Class — Core Differences
questions.direct_answer: The key difference is **state and inheritance**: an **abstract class** can hold **instance fields**, **constructors**, and concrete methods, but a class can extend only **one**. An **interface** is a pure **contract** with **no instance state** (only `public static final` constants), but a class can implement **many**. Abstract class = shared base with state; interface = capability multiple types can have.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can name the decisive differences (state, single vs multiple inheritance) and choose correctly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating outdated 'interfaces can't have method bodies' (false since Java 8) or missing the instance-state distinction.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame as IS-A shared base vs CAN-DO capability, note interfaces have only public static final constants (no instance variables), and that an interface can extend another interface.

sections.title: From Zero: A Contract vs a Half-Built Parent
sections.content:
An **interface** is a contract that lists the methods a class must have; an **abstract class** is a partly-built parent class that other classes finish. Both let you declare methods without writing every body, so a beginner often treats them as the same tool — they aren't.

They exist for **two different jobs**. An abstract class is for when several classes are the *same kind of thing* and want to share real code and data — a `Shape` base that already stores a `color` field and has a working `getColor()`, leaving only `area()` for each shape to fill in. An interface is for when you only want to promise a behavior, with no shared code or data behind it — `Comparable` just says 'this type can be compared.'

**How each one works decides everything:**

- An `abstract class` is a true class, so it can hold **instance fields**, **constructors**, and a mix of finished and unfinished methods — but a class can `extend` only **one** of them.
- An `interface` holds **no instance state**: every field is silently `public static final` (a constant), and there are no constructors, so a class can `implement` **many** at once.

Since Java 8 an interface can also carry `default` and `static` methods that *do* have bodies, and one interface can `extend` several others.

The real interview decision is about **state, not syntax**: choose an abstract class when there's genuine shared data or code to inherit, otherwise choose an interface. The gotcha that dates a candidate is saying 'interfaces can't have method bodies' — false since Java 8. The line that still holds is that interfaces can't hold instance state.

> **Rule of thumb:** reach for an `abstract class` only when there's real shared state or code to inherit — otherwise default to an `interface`.

sections.title: Interface vs Abstract Class — Side by Side
sections.content:
| Aspect | Interface | Abstract Class |
|---|---|---|
| **Instance state (fields)** | No — only `public static final` constants | Yes — instance fields allowed |
| **Constructors** | No | Yes |
| **Method bodies** | `default`/`static`/`private` (Java 8+) | Concrete + abstract |
| **How many** | A class can implement **many** | A class can extend **one** |
| **Keyword used** | `implements` (class); `extends` (interface) | `extends` |
| **Can extend others** | Yes — an interface can extend multiple interfaces | Yes — abstract class extends one class |
| **Models** | CAN-DO capability | IS-A shared base |
| **When to choose** | Capability, multiple roles, decoupling | Shared state + concrete code in one family |

sections.title: Single Inheritance vs Multiple Interface Implementation
sections.content:
The diagram below shows the asymmetry: a class can climb only one class hierarchy, but it can absorb capabilities from many interfaces at once. ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph ClassHierarchy["Class hierarchy — single inheritance"] AC["abstract class Shape
(color field, getColor, abstract area)"] --> Circle AC --> Rectangle end subgraph Interfaces["Interface capabilities — multiple allowed"] I1["interface Drawable
void draw()"] I2["interface Resizable
void resize(double factor)"] I3["interface Serializable
(marker)"] end Circle["class Circle"] -->|implements| I1 Circle -->|implements| I2 Circle -->|implements| I3 subgraph InterfaceExtends["Interfaces can extend interfaces"] IBase["interface Readable"] IBase2["interface Writable"] ICombo["interface ReadWrite
extends Readable, Writable"] IBase --> ICombo IBase2 --> ICombo end ``` `Circle` extends one abstract class (`Shape`) but implements three interfaces simultaneously. Meanwhile, `ReadWrite` shows how an interface can extend multiple parent interfaces — building up a richer contract from simpler ones.

sections.title: Both Patterns Together — Java 17
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Abstract class**: instance fields + constructors + concrete/abstract methods; a class extends **one**.
- **Interface**: no instance variables — only `public static final` constants; no constructors; a class implements **many**.
- **'Interfaces have no bodies' is outdated** — since Java 8, `default` and `static` methods have bodies; the real difference is the absence of *instance state*.
- **Interface can extend another interface** (or multiple) using `extends` — this is how `List extends Collection extends Iterable`.
- Abstract class = **IS-A** shared base; interface = **CAN-DO** capability.
- A class can **combine both**: extend one abstract class and implement many interfaces simultaneously.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Saying 'interfaces can't have method bodies'** — this has been false since Java 8 added `default` and `static` methods, and it instantly signals you learned Java from a pre-2014 article.
- **Treating interface fields as variables** — every field is implicitly `public static final`, so it's a shared constant; trying to use one as per-object state simply won't compile.
- **Thinking you must pick one or the other** — a class can `extend` one abstract class *and* `implement` many interfaces at the same time, and missing this leads to needlessly rigid designs.
- **Defaulting to an abstract class just to reuse code** — that burns your single inheritance slot; when there's no shared instance state, an interface with `default` methods reuses code without the cost.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The cleanest way to separate them is **by state, not by method bodies**. An abstract class is a real class, so it can hold instance fields and a constructor and share concrete code — but you only get to `extend` **one**. An interface carries no per-object state; its fields are quietly `public static final` constants, and because nothing travels with it, a class can `implement` as many as it wants.

One thing I'd avoid is saying interfaces have no method bodies — **that's been false since Java 8** gave them `default` and `static` methods. The real divide is **instance state**. I think of an abstract class as an **IS-A shared base** and an interface as a **CAN-DO capability** that even unrelated types can have — and an interface can even `extend` several other interfaces.

So my default is **interface-first**; I reach for an abstract class only when there's genuine shared state or code to inherit.

questions.question: Why can a class implement multiple interfaces but only extend one class in Java?
questions.title: Multiple Interface Implementation vs Single Class Inheritance
questions.direct_answer: A class can implement **many interfaces** but extend only **one class** because interfaces carry **no instance state** (no fields, no constructors), so combining them creates no conflict. Multiple **classes** would bring conflicting fields, constructors, and method implementations — the **diamond problem** — which Java avoids by allowing only single class inheritance.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you connect 'multiple interfaces, one class' to the absence of state in interfaces and the diamond problem.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Stating the rule without the reason, or thinking default methods make interfaces as risky as classes.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain default-method conflicts are resolvable (override + InterfaceName.super), but conflicting state from multiple classes is not, which is the real blocker.

sections.title: From Zero: Why One Path Brings Conflict and the Other Doesn't
sections.content:
A class in Java can `implement` as many interfaces as you list, but it can `extend` only **one** class. Stated that baldly it sounds like an arbitrary rule — the interesting part is *why* the two are treated so differently.

The whole answer is **state**. A class carries instance fields, constructors, and method bodies. Picture `class Duck extends Bird, Fish` being allowed:

- If both parents have a field named `sound`, which one does `duck.sound` mean?
- Both parents have their own constructor chain — which runs first?
- If both define `move()`, whose body wins?

There is no unambiguous answer, and this tangle has a name: the **diamond problem**.

Interfaces sidestep all of it because they hold **nothing per-object**. Before Java 8 an interface was just method signatures — no fields, no constructors — so stacking ten of them creates nothing to collide, and the implementing class supplies one clear body for each method.

Here's the **interview nuance most freshers miss**. Java 8 added `default` methods that *do* have bodies, so two interfaces *can* declare the same `default move()`. But that clash is **resolvable**: the compiler simply forces you to override it, and inside the override you can still reach either parent's version with `InterfaceName.super.move()`. The gotcha is concluding that default methods make interfaces as dangerous as classes — they don't. A method-body clash has a clean fix; conflicting instance state from two parent classes has none. That missing fix is the real reason the asymmetry exists.

> **The real blocker is state:** a `default`-method clash has a clean fix, but conflicting instance state from two parent classes has none — so only class inheritance is limited to one.

sections.title: Why the Rules Are Different
sections.content:
| Source of conflict | Multiple classes | Multiple interfaces |
|---|---|---|
| **Instance fields** | Conflict — same name from two parents is ambiguous | No conflict — interfaces have no instance fields |
| **Constructors** | Two chains to run — which super() wins? | No conflict — interfaces have no constructors |
| **Method bodies** | Ambiguous if both parents define same method | `default` clash is resolvable via override + `X.super.method()` |
| **Resolution available?** | No clean resolution — diamond problem | Yes — compiler forces override |
| **Java rule** | Extend **one** class only | Implement **many** interfaces |

sections.title: The Diamond Problem — Why It Blocks Multiple Class Inheritance
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph Illegal["Multiple class inheritance — NOT allowed"] B["class Bird
String sound = 'tweet'
void move() { fly }"] F["class Fish
String sound = 'blub'
void move() { swim }"] D_bad["class Duck extends Bird, Fish
❌ Which sound? Which move? Which constructor?"] B --> D_bad F --> D_bad end subgraph Legal["Multiple interface implementation — allowed"] IF["interface Flyer
default String move() { return 'fly' }"] IS["interface Swimmer
default String move() { return 'swim' }"] D_good["class Duck implements Flyer, Swimmer
✅ Override move() — pick one or combine
Flyer.super.move() + Swimmer.super.move()"] IF --> D_good IS --> D_good end ``` With classes the conflict is unresolvable (fields, constructors, state). With interfaces a `default` method clash just triggers a compiler error that you fix by overriding — a clean, explicit resolution.

sections.title: Multiple Interfaces + Resolving a Default Method Clash — Java 17
Key Points
sections.content:
- Multiple class inheritance creates **unresolvable** conflicts: competing fields, constructors, and method bodies — the diamond problem.
- Interfaces have **no instance state and no constructors**, so combining many is conflict-free.
- Java allows exactly **one** parent class but **many** implemented interfaces.
- `default` method clashes from multiple interfaces are **resolvable**: the compiler forces an override, and you call the chosen parent's version via `InterfaceName.super.method()`.
- The real blocker is conflicting **state** — only classes carry state, which is why only class inheritance is restricted to one.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Stating the rule without the reason** — 'a class extends one but implements many' is only the *what*; interviewers want 'because interfaces carry no instance state,' and stopping short reads as memorization.
- **Believing default methods make interfaces as risky as classes** — a `default` method clash is resolvable with an override, while conflicting fields from two parent classes are not, which is the actual blocker.
- **Forgetting how to resolve a default clash** — when two interfaces define the same `default`, you must override it and call `InterfaceName.super.method()`; saying 'it just fails' misses the fix interviewers listen for.
- **Blaming method bodies for the diamond problem** — the unsolvable conflict is duplicated state and constructor chains, not the mere existence of method bodies; mislabeling it exposes a shallow grasp.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The rule is easy to state — a class `implements` many interfaces but `extends` only one class — but what the interviewer really wants is the reason, and **the reason is state**. A class carries instance fields, constructors, and method bodies. If Java let you extend two classes and both had a field called `sound`, the JVM couldn't know which one you mean; both bring their own constructor chain, so it's unclear which runs first; and if both implemented the same method, there's no answer for whose body wins. That unsolvable tangle is the **diamond problem**, and it's why extending more than one class is banned.

Interfaces don't have any of that. They hold no fields and no constructors, so implementing five or twenty of them creates nothing to collide — the implementing class is the **single source of state** and gives one body per method. The subtlety worth raising is `default` methods: since Java 8 two interfaces can declare the same `default` method, which is a real clash. But it's **resolvable** — the compiler forces you to override it, and inside that override you can still call either parent with `Flyer.super.move()`. So I'd push back on the idea that default methods make interfaces as risky as classes. **A method-body clash has a clean fix; conflicting instance state from two parent classes doesn't** — and that missing fix is the whole reason the asymmetry exists.

questions.question: When should you use an interface versus an abstract class in Java?
questions.title: Choosing Between Interface and Abstract Class in Java
questions.direct_answer: Use an **interface** to define a **capability** that many (even unrelated) types can have, when you need **multiple inheritance of type**, or to decouple callers from implementations. Use an **abstract class** when related subclasses **share state and concrete code** and you want a common base with a template. Default to interfaces; reach for an abstract class when shared implementation/state is real.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can pick the right tool based on shared state vs capability and multiple-type needs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Always using abstract classes for code sharing, or creating an interface where no variation/abstraction is needed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention you can combine both — an interface for the contract plus an abstract base providing partial implementation (e.g. AbstractList implements List).

sections.title: From Zero: Capability vs a Shared Base
sections.content:
Use an **interface** to say *what a type can do*, and an **abstract class** to give related types a shared, half-finished base they all build on. At first they feel interchangeable because both let you leave methods unimplemented — the choice only becomes clear once you ask what you're really modeling.

Both exist to solve **different problems**. An interface captures a **capability** — `Runnable`, `Comparable`, `Iterable` — something even completely unrelated types can promise to do without sharing anything else. An abstract class captures a **family** — a `Shape` whose `Circle` and `Rectangle` are clearly the same kind of thing and genuinely share data and code.

**How each one works points you to the right choice:**

- An `abstract class` can hold **instance fields**, a **constructor**, and concrete helper methods — perfect when subclasses share a field like `color` or use a **template method** that fixes an algorithm and leaves a few holes for subclasses to fill.
- An `interface` holds no state, but a class can `implement` **many** of them — so it's the tool when a type must play several roles, or when callers should depend on a contract and swap implementations freely.

The interview-grade rule is to default to an interface and reach for an abstract class only when there is *real* shared state or code to inherit — because committing to a base class spends your one inheritance slot. The mark of maturity is knowing you can do both at once: define the contract as an interface and supply a skeletal abstract base beside it, exactly how the JDK pairs `List` with `AbstractList`. The gotcha is reflexively grabbing an abstract class just to reuse code — interface `default` methods often share that code without locking anyone into a hierarchy.

> **Default to an `interface`;** reach for an `abstract class` only when there's *real* shared state or code to inherit — and remember you can do both, exactly how the JDK pairs `List` with `AbstractList`.

sections.title: Pick the Right Tool
sections.content:
| Situation | Use | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Capability many unrelated types should have | **Interface** | `Runnable`, `Comparable`, `Printable` — any type can implement |
| A type needs to play multiple roles | **Interface** | A class can implement many interfaces, extend only one class |
| Callers should depend on a contract, swap impls | **Interface** | `List` ref works for `ArrayList` or `LinkedList` |
| Subclasses share instance fields | **Abstract class** | Only abstract classes can hold per-object state |
| Subclasses share concrete code (template method) | **Abstract class** | Common algorithm in base, abstract holes for subclasses |
| Both contract + partial implementation | **Interface + abstract base** | e.g. `List` interface + `AbstractList` skeletal impl |

sections.title: Interface for Capability, Abstract Class for Shared State — Java 17
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Use an interface** for capabilities (`Runnable`, `Comparable`), when unrelated types share a behavior, when a type needs multiple roles, or when you want callers decoupled from implementations.
- **Use an abstract class** when related subclasses share instance fields, constructors, and concrete code — especially for the template method pattern.
- **Default to interface-first** — it's more flexible; add an abstract class only when shared state or implementation is real.
- **Combine them** when you need both: define the contract in an interface, provide a skeletal implementation in an abstract base (`AbstractList implements List`).
- A class can implement **many** interfaces but extend only **one** abstract class — so committing to an abstract base early is a bigger restriction.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reaching for an abstract class just to share code** — it spends the single inheritance slot; an interface with `default` methods often reuses the same code without locking subclasses into a hierarchy.
- **Creating an interface where there's no variation** — adding a contract with exactly one implementation and no second type in sight is needless indirection, not flexibility.
- **Not knowing you can combine both** — the `AbstractList implements List` pattern (contract plus skeletal base) is what interviewers look for; missing it makes you sound like you only know one tool.
- **Choosing by keyword instead of by design** — the decision is about shared state versus capability, not `implements` versus `extends`; picking by habit leads to rigid hierarchies you can't extend later.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I treat this as a **design decision rather than a syntax one**, and I start by asking what I'm modeling. If it's a **capability** — something a type can do, like `Runnable` or `Comparable` — I use an interface, because even unrelated types can implement it and a class can implement as many as it needs. Interfaces are also right when callers should depend on a contract and swap implementations, so a `List` reference works whether it's backed by an `ArrayList` or a `LinkedList`.

I reach for an **abstract class** only when a group of subclasses are clearly the same kind of thing and genuinely share state and code — a common `color` or `id` field, a shared helper, or a **template method** where the base fixes the algorithm and leaves a couple of holes for each subclass. `HttpServlet` is the classic example: the lifecycle lives in the base and you just override `doGet` or `doPost`.

What I'd avoid is grabbing an abstract class just to reuse code, since that spends your one inheritance slot — `default` methods often share code without that cost. So my default is **interface-first**, and the thing I'd add is that these aren't either-or: you can define the contract as an interface and provide a skeletal abstract base alongside it, which is exactly what `AbstractList` does for `List` in the JDK.
